archetype.name: Gunslinger (scheme-managed)
archetype.definition: A big-armed, historically turnover-prone passer whose career has swung on accuracy. In Seattle's run-first, under-center game he has been kept on schedule and pointed at one dominant receiver.

report.headline: Brilliant two-game efficiency from a career-long inaccurate passer, now back on the bench
report.take:
Drew Lock's 2026 line looks like a top-five starter's. He is third among 47 qualifiers in EPA per dropback (0.451) and in adjusted net yards per dropback (10.5), seventh in CPOE, and has no interceptions. He is also Seattle's QB2 again. Sam Darnold started Weeks 7 and 8 after Lock's run in the lineup, and Lock was a coach's-decision inactive this week with an elbow listed. The dossier's play-by-play covers only two of his games, 48 charted attempts. Read everything below as a strong small sample from a backup, not a new baseline.

What drove it is clear. The first driver is Jaxon Smith-Njigba. His 21 targets added 24.7 EPA, slightly more than all 51 of Lock's dropbacks combined (24.3). Every other target was roughly a wash, and Rashid Shaheed's eight were clearly negative. The second is structure. Under center, Lock went 100% on 14 attempts with 0.891 EPA a play and an 80% success rate. From shotgun his CPOE was -2.5 and his success rate 0.371. That shotgun version looks a lot more like the Lock of 2020-2024. The third is a soft schedule spot: his best game, 16.1 EPA and three touchdowns, came in a 31-7 rout of an Arizona defense now ranked 27th.

The career record is the reality check. Lock's CPOE was negative in every prior season: -0.8, -5.5, -3.3, -5.1 and -6.1. His bad-throw rates ran in the 16-22% range, and he threw 15 interceptions in 13 games in 2020. This year's 12.5% bad-throw rate and zero turnover-worthy plays are a genuine improvement over two games. A two-game run doesn't overturn five seasons of evidence, though, and five deep attempts producing 9.9 EPA is the kind of split that evaporates. The scheme deserves real credit. Seattle limits his aggressiveness: his average throw lands 1.25 yards short of the sticks, and the team passes 6.5 points below expectation. That keeps the risk down, but it doesn't change who he is.

Going forward, his value is as insurance. If Darnold misses time, Lock walks into a good situation: a top-five defense that keeps games close or comfortable, a run game that forces play-action looks, and Smith-Njigba. Expect competent, low-volume starts with efficiency somewhere between this year's line and his career norms. The interceptions will likely start coming back.

strengths.title: Under-center, play-action efficiency
strengths.body: Seattle's under-center looks turned Lock into a near-perfect passer on those snaps: 14 of 14 with 0.891 EPA a play. Those designs give him defined reads and clean windows, which shields his accuracy issues. That edge belongs to the scheme, so it carries into any future start, though not at a 100% clip.

strengths.title: Feeding Smith-Njigba
strengths.body: Lock's production runs through one receiver: Smith-Njigba's 24.7 EPA on 21 targets exceeds Lock's entire dropback total. Knowing where the ball should go is a skill, and that connection will be there in any start. It does mean his efficiency depends on a single target being open.

strengths.title: Clean ball security, so far
strengths.body: He has no interceptions and no turnover-worthy plays, and his sack rate (4%) is well below the league's 6.9%. Some of that comes from the conservative aim point and a run-first plan. Some of it is a two-game sample that his 2020 season says won't hold.

concerns.title: Accuracy runs against his career
concerns.body: A +6.72 CPOE from a passer who was negative in all five previous seasons is almost certainly mostly noise and scheme. When the offense put him in shotgun and asked him to drive the ball, his CPOE fell to -2.5 and his success rate to 0.371. That shotgun version is the likelier one in a longer stretch.

concerns.title: He's the backup again
concerns.body: Darnold reclaimed the job for Weeks 7 and 8, and Lock was inactive as a coach's decision with an elbow on the report. His rest-of-season value hinges entirely on someone else's health. If the elbow lingers, he may not even be the active QB2.

concerns.title: Line protection is thinning
concerns.body: Seattle's offense ranks 29th in hit rate allowed. Charles Cross, the left tackle who plays 98% of snaps, is out. Lock's 22.2% pressure-to-sack rate is only middling, and he would take any emergency snaps behind a weakened edge.

trend.note: On the field he climbed from 6.4 EPA against New England to 16.1 against Arizona. His role has since gone the other way, from starter back to QB2 behind Darnold.

nextGame.headline: A soft matchup he likely won't get to use
nextGame.body:
On paper this is the best setup a passer can draw. Arizona ranks 31st in pass EPA allowed, 30th in explosive pass rate and 24th against deep throws. It gives up 22 PPR points a game to quarterbacks, 31st in the league. Lock carved this same defense for 235 yards and three touchdowns in Week 2. With Seattle an 11.5-point favorite, any snaps he does get would likely be late in a comfortable win.

Availability decides everything. Lock is listed out with an elbow, with a projected return of game day, and was a coach's-decision inactive last week. He gets on the field only if Darnold gets hurt or the game becomes a blowout. On his side, Cross (left tackle) and Shaheed are out. Arizona is without DT Walter Nolen III, a 62%-snap player, which helps any Seattle quarterback.

keyMatchups.title: Arizona's leaky pass defense
keyMatchups.body: The Cardinals allow 0.269 EPA a dropback and rank 30th in explosive pass rate. That is the same unit Lock picked apart in Week 2. If he plays, efficiency should be strong.

keyMatchups.title: Smith-Njigba against Arizona's WR1 coverage
keyMatchups.body: Arizona allows 0.67 EPA a target to opposing WR1s, 30th in the league. That is exactly where Lock's offense lives.

keyMatchups.title: Blowout script
keyMatchups.body: The Book has Seattle at -11.5, and Seattle's defense ranks fifth in EPA. A lopsided game is the most plausible path to garbage-time snaps for the backup.

nextGame.watch: Whether Lock is active as QB2 and whether the elbow is still a factor.

restOfSeason.body:
As long as Darnold is healthy, Lock's projection is close to zero snaps. The ranges below are per start if he is pressed into duty. The volume should stay modest, since Seattle passes well below expectation, and the defense should keep scripts manageable. The parts that should carry over are the under-center designs, the Smith-Njigba connection and the conservative throw depth.

What won't hold is the accuracy and the clean sheet. A career-long negative-CPOE passer posting +6.72, with zero interceptions and a deep-ball split built on five throws, will drift back toward something like 0.05-0.15 EPA per dropback over real volume. Interceptions will reappear at roughly one every start or two.

confidence.note: Two charted games, a backup role, and an elbow issue.
